:::{#thm-linear-map-matrix}
#### Every linear map is multiplication by a matrix

If $f: \reals^p \to \reals^m$ is a linear map (@def-linear-map),
then there is exactly one $m \times p$ matrix $\matr{A}$ such that

$$f(\vx) = \matr{A}\vx \quad \text{for all } \vx \in \reals^p$$

Column $j$ of $\matr{A}$ is $f(\vecf{e}_j)$,
the image of the $j$th indicator vector (@def-indicator-vector);
that is, $a_{ij} = \paren{f(\vecf{e}_j)}_i$.
$\matr{A}$ is called the **matrix of** $f$.

:::

::: proof

**Existence.** Let $\matr{A}$ be the $m \times p$ matrix with
$a_{ij} = \paren{f(\vecf{e}_j)}_i$.
For any $\vx \in \reals^p$,

$$
\ba
f(\vx)
&= f\paren{\sum_{j=1}^{p} x_j \vecf{e}_j}
&& \text{(@thm-standard-basis-expansion)}
\\&= \sum_{j=1}^{p} x_j f(\vecf{e}_j)
&& \text{(@thm-linear-map-lincom)}
\ea
$$

and entry $i$ of that sum is

$$
\ba
\paren{\sum_{j=1}^{p} x_j f(\vecf{e}_j)}_i
&= \sum_{j=1}^{p} x_j \paren{f(\vecf{e}_j)}_i
&& \text{(@def-linear-combination, entry by entry)}
\\&= \sum_{j=1}^{p} x_j a_{ij}
&& \text{(definition of } \matr{A} \text{)}
\\&= \sum_{j=1}^{p} a_{ij} x_j
&& \text{(products are symmetric)}
\\&= (\matr{A}\vx)_i
&& \text{(@def-matvec-mult)}
\ea
$$

**Uniqueness.** Suppose $\matr{B}$ is any $m \times p$ matrix
with $f(\vx) = \matr{B}\vx$ for all $\vx$.
Taking $\vx = \vecf{e}_j$, for each $i$:

$$
\ba
\paren{f(\vecf{e}_j)}_i
&= (\matr{B}\vecf{e}_j)_i
&& \text{(assumption on } \matr{B} \text{)}
\\&= \sum_{k=1}^{p} b_{ik} (\vecf{e}_j)_k
&& \text{(@def-matvec-mult)}
\\&= b_{ij}
&& \text{(only the } k = j \text{ term is nonzero; @def-indicator-vector)}
\ea
$$

So $b_{ij} = \paren{f(\vecf{e}_j)}_i = a_{ij}$ for every $i$ and $j$,
and $\matr{B} = \matr{A}$.

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#exm-linear-map-matrix}
#### Finding the matrix of a linear map

For $f(\vx) = (2 x_1,\ x_1 + x_2)$ from @exm-linear-map,
the images of the indicator vectors are

$$
f(\vecf{e}_1) = f\paren{\sbmat{1 \\ 0}} = \sbmat{2 \cd 1 \\ 1 + 0} = \sbmat{2 \\ 1},
\qquad
f(\vecf{e}_2) = f\paren{\sbmat{0 \\ 1}} = \sbmat{2 \cd 0 \\ 0 + 1} = \sbmat{0 \\ 1}
$$

and these are the columns of the matrix of $f$:
$\matr{A} = \sbmat{2 & 0 \\ 1 & 1}$.

:::
